title: Paying Yourself as a Solo Founder (Without Going Broke) | Indie Money 31

description:

Which is a weirdly hard question.
It's a weirdly hard question, and we both got it wrong for years, so we're going to be honest about that.
Very honest, I have a tax story that still haunts me.
Okay, we'll save the tax story, but real quick before we get into it, let's take a quick break to thank our sponsors.

Okay, paying yourself.
So the first mistake, and I did this for two years, is paying yourself whatever's left at the end of the month.
Which sounds reasonable.
It sounds totally reasonable, and it's a disaster, because some months there's nothing left, and some months there's a lot, and you spend the lot.
You spend the lot, and then the next bad month you're scrambling.
So what we both do now is a fixed amount, even if it's small.
Like, when my business was making about four thousand a month, I paid myself fifteen hundred, every month, same day.
And the rest?
The rest goes into what we call the three buckets.
Bucket one is taxes, and you move that money out first, before you touch anything else.
For me in the US that's around twenty-five to thirty percent of profit, but your number is your number, ask an accountant.
Bucket two is a runway fund, so the business can survive a few bad months without you skipping your own pay.
And bucket three is the stuff the business needs, tools, contractors, a new laptop when the old one dies.
How big should the runway fund be, though, because people always ask that.
I'd say start with three months of your own pay plus the fixed costs, and grow it to six when you can.
And the important thing is, the runway fund is not a shopping fund.
It is not a shopping fund, Rosa, I know, I know.
I'm not looking at anyone in particular.
You're looking directly at me.
The other thing that helped me was picking a payday and treating it like a real job, so I pay myself on the first, every month, no matter what.
And when you have a great month?
When I have a great month, the extra goes into the runway fund first, and only once that's full do I give myself a raise.
Okay, Kwame, I think it's time for the tax story.
Fine, so, my first good year, I was so excited about the revenue that I completely forgot quarterly estimated taxes existed.
Completely forgot.
Completely, and then April comes, and I owe this huge amount, plus a penalty, plus I've already spent most of it on a fancy standing desk.
The standing desk!
The standing desk, which I now stand at every day and think about my mistakes.
It's a very expensive reminder.
It's a very expensive reminder, and that's why the tax bucket comes first, no exceptions.
What do you do now, practically, so it doesn't happen again?
Every time a payment comes in, I move thirty percent into a separate savings account the same day, before I even look at it.
Same day, and it has a different bank, so it's slightly annoying to get to.
Slightly annoying is the whole strategy, I don't trust myself.
So, one listener question before we wrap.
This is from Inés, who asks, should I pay myself a salary through payroll or just take owner's draws?
Honestly, it depends on how your business is set up, and this is exactly the kind of thing where an hour with an accountant pays for itself.
Yeah, we can tell you what we do, but your situation is different from ours.
Okay, that's the episode, go set up your three buckets this week.
And please, please remember your quarterly taxes.
Bye everyone.
